---
title: "Local development with oxyc proxy"
description: "Run a custom app on your machine against a real cloud Oxy's data, so you can verify you're getting the right results before you publish."
---

When you build a **custom app** (a React/Vite bundle you ship with `oxyc publish`),
you usually want to run it locally with `pnpm dev` — but a local app has no Oxy
identity, no auth, and no data. `oxyc proxy` closes that gap: it lets your local
app call a **real cloud Oxy** and return real data, so you can confirm your
queries, charts, and functions work *before* you publish.

It's the same idea as `vercel dev` or Cloudflare's remote bindings: **your code
runs locally, your data comes from the cloud.**

`oxyc` is Oxy's command-line client. Install it once:

```bash
npm install -g @oxy-hq/cli
```

## How it works

`oxyc proxy` starts a small local **proxy on port 3000** — exactly where a local
`oxy serve` would run. Your dev server keeps serving your app (with hot reload
untouched) and forwards its Oxy calls to the proxy, which attaches your
`oxyc login` token and forwards them to the cloud environment you chose.

```text
  browser ──▶ pnpm dev (:5173, serves your app + hot reload)
                  │  Oxy calls ↓
                  ▼
            oxyc proxy (:3000)  ── adds your token ──▶  cloud (--env dev)
```

Because the proxy sits on port 3000, the `@oxy-hq/vite-plugin` — whose default
Oxy target is already `localhost:3000` — needs **no configuration**. Your app
just starts hitting cloud data.

<Note>
  Your token stays inside the `oxyc proxy` process. It is added to requests
  server-side and is never exposed to browser JavaScript or written to a `.env`.
</Note>

## Quick start

<Steps>
  <Step title="Log in to the environment you want data from">
    ```bash
    oxyc login --env dev
    ```
    This caches a token per environment (`dev`, `staging`, `production`, or a
    deployment URL). Use the environment whose data you want to develop against.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Start the proxy">
    ```bash
    # run from your custom app's directory (it reads oxy-app.json for the target)
    oxyc proxy --env dev
    ```
    You'll see a banner confirming the target and the active guardrails.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Start your app as usual">
    ```bash
    pnpm dev
    ```
    Open your dev server (e.g. `http://localhost:5173`). Your app now shows real
    data from the `dev` environment.
  </Step>
</Steps>

## What you can access

`oxyc proxy` forwards requests with **your own** `oxyc login` token, so you can only
reach data you're already allowed to see. Access to an app's data is granted if
you are:

- a **member** of the app's organization, or
- an **Oxy app-admin**, or
- a **partner admin** with the *manage apps* capability over the org's partner
  (so a partner's developers can build against their managed orgs without being
  org members).

If you aren't authorized for the app's org, requests return `403` — the same rule
the deployed app enforces.

## Guardrails

Because you may be pointing at a real (possibly production) environment, side
effects are off by default:

| Behavior | Default | Opt in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Usage/tracking events | **dropped** (won't pollute the target's analytics) | `--allow-events` |
| Functions (`/fn`), agent runs, automation runs | **held** — rejected with `409` until you opt in | `--allow-writes` |
| Pointing at a production host (anything on `oxygen-hq.com`, including an org's own subdomain) | **refused** | `--yes` |

Reads — `query` and `semantic-query` — are always forwarded; those are what you
need to "validate the data."

<Warning>
  `--allow-writes` and `--yes` let your local app trigger real function/agent
  executions on the target environment. Use them deliberately, and prefer a `dev`
  or `staging` env over `production`.
</Warning>

## Debugging a function call

Every Oxy Function call through the proxy carries a trace — the one the SDK
started, or one the proxy starts for it — and prints a line with the ids to look
up when it fails:

```text
  ↳ 500 fn refresh  request_id=0f3c…  trace_id=4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736
```

Quote the `trace_id` when you ask for help. When the call came from
`@oxy-hq/sdk`, it is also the `traceId` on the error your app received.

## Options

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--env <name\|url>` | Environment to resolve the target + token from (same as `oxyc login --env`): a name from `oxy-app.json` `environments`, `dev` / `staging` / `production`, or a deployment URL. Defaults to `production`. |
| `--target <url>` | Explicit Oxy base URL; overrides `--env`. |
| `--port <n>` | Local port (default **3000**). Change it if 3000 is taken — then point your dev server's Oxy proxy at the new port. |
| `--allow-events` | Forward tracking events instead of dropping them. |
| `--allow-writes` | Forward `/fn`, agent, and automation calls instead of holding them. |
| `--yes` | Confirm proxying to a production host. |
| `--token-env <var>` | Read the token from this environment variable instead of `OXY_TOKEN` (the cached login is the fallback). |

## Troubleshooting

**`no cached token for <target>`** — the proxy still starts, but only requests that
carry their own sign-in will work. Run `oxyc login --env <env>` for the same
environment you pass to `oxyc proxy`.

**`port 3000 is already in use`** — something is already on port 3000 (often a
local `oxy serve`). Stop it, or run `oxyc proxy --port <n>` and point your dev
server's Oxy proxy at that port.

**`refusing to proxy to a production target`** — the target is a production host.
Pass `--yes` if that is really what you want, or use `--env dev`.

**`409` with `held_by_oxyc_proxy`** — your app called a function / agent /
automation. Re-run with `--allow-writes` if you intend those to execute against
the target.

**Empty or `403` responses** — you may not be authorized for the app's
organization. Confirm you're a member, an app-admin, or a partner admin with
*manage apps* over that org.
